items.prompt: A radio report says the world's economies have grown closer through trade, travel and technology. Define globalisation.
items.canonical_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies: trade in goods and services across borders widens, companies spread production and sales across several countries, and information, finance and people move between countries more freely. It is a process, not a single event.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state the growing integration of the world's economies and name what moves between countries - goods and services, companies operating across borders, information, finance and people.
A definition that names a single cause, such as technology alone, is partial credit at most: the term covers trade, companies and the movement of people and information together.

items.prompt: At a supermarket in Oshakati a learner finds rice from Vietnam, a phone designed in Japan, and a banking app that moves money to a cousin studying in Portugal. Identify two features of globalisation these examples show.
items.canonical_answer: First, goods produced in one country and sold in others: the rice from Vietnam and the phone designed in Japan crossed borders to reach the shelf. Second, information and finance moving worldwide: the banking app sends money between Namibia and Portugal in seconds.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark per feature of globalisation identified from the scenario, tied to the example that shows it.

What it includes: the features the examples can support are trade across borders, companies producing in several countries, and information and finance moving worldwide - a feature named without its example earns partial credit at most.

items.prompt: Haneda Electronics keeps its head office in Japan and runs assembly plants in Oshakati and in Brazil. Define a multinational company.
items.canonical_answer: A multinational company is a firm that produces goods or services in more than one country, through operations it runs there; selling abroad from home is exporting. Its head-office country is home, the others are hosts: here Japan is home, Namibia and Brazil hosts.
marking_guidance: Definition: the precise meaning required is producing in more than one country, through operations the firm runs there (selling abroad from home is exporting), with the home country named as the head office country and the others as host countries.

The boundary to insist on: a multinational company is defined by where it operates, not by ownership - a public limited company sells shares on a stock exchange, a state-owned company belongs to a government, and the same firm may be multinational and either of these. The test is which question the sentence answers: ownership traded, who owns it, or where it operates.

items.prompt: Marula Foods of Windhoek is considering opening a jam factory near Lisbon in Portugal. Explain why producing in another country may suit the firm.
items.canonical_answer: Producing near Lisbon may lower costs, where wages and fruit there are cheaper than making jam in Namibia and shipping it. It puts the factory close to European buyers, so transport costs and delivery times fall. And producing inside the region makes a wider market easier to reach, because the firm serves customers directly and can respond to their tastes faster. Each reason is about what the location does for the firm: lower costs, closer customers and a larger market.
marking_guidance: Reasons: award one mark per reason and one for its development with a because link - lower costs, closer customers, transport savings, or wider markets.
Why: the reason must be the firm's purpose, not a fact about Portugal - a developed reason states what the location does for the firm.

items.prompt: Haneda Electronics, with its head office in Japan, employs 300 workers at its new Oshakati plant at an average N$6 500 a month and has trained 60 technicians whose skills are now used by other firms in the town. Its profits, about N$12 million a year, are paid to the head office. Explain what the figures suggest about the effects of this multinational company on its host country and on its home country.
items.canonical_answer: Namibia, the host, gains jobs and skills: 300 x N$6 500 = N$1 950 000 a month in wages reaches Oshakati households, and because the 60 trained technicians also work for other firms, know-how spreads beyond the plant. But about N$12 million of profit a year goes to the head office, so part of the value created in Namibia leaves. For Japan, the home country, that profit is a gain, though the 300 jobs were created abroad rather than at home.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must work from the figures - the 300 jobs at N$6 500, the 60 technicians, and the N$12 million profit - rather than from general knowledge of multinational companies.
Reasoning: each effect needs its because link - jobs and wages because the plant employs locally, skills because training spreads to other firms, outflow because profit is paid to the head office.

Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean for the host country - gains in jobs, wages and skills, alongside profit leaving - and for the home country, which receives the profit but not the jobs.

items.prompt: After Namibia ended its border taxes on imported shoes, a learner says the shoes are now free goods. Define free trade.
items.canonical_answer: Free trade is international trade without government barriers: no tariffs, import quotas or embargoes. Free refers to the absence of barriers, not to price: the shoes still cost money, so they are not free goods, which are so abundant that taking them costs nothing.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state international trade without barriers - tariffs, import quotas and embargoes - and may add that free refers to the barriers rather than to price.

The confusion to correct: free trade is a border policy while a free good is a good with no opportunity cost; the test is whether the sentence is about what happens at the border or about what the good costs. The learner in the prompt has run the two together.

items.prompt: Explain why consumers in Namibia tend to gain when the country trades freely.
items.canonical_answer: Consumers tend to gain lower prices, because imports entering without tariffs or quotas compete with home goods and competition pulls prices down: a cheaper import on the next shelf makes the home blanket cheaper too. They also gain wider choice, because free trade brings goods the country does not make, or makes in few varieties. These are benefits to individuals as consumers; separately, producers gain cheaper inputs and larger markets, and the economy gains as resources shift towards what Namibia produces best.
marking_guidance: Reasons: award one mark per reason - lower prices through import competition, wider choice - and one for its development with a because link.

The level to keep: these are benefits to individuals as consumers, which differ from benefits to the country as a whole - the answer should name who gains, and a response about the whole economy answers a different question.

items.prompt: Before Namibia removed a tariff, imported blankets cost N$250 each and home blankets N$240. After the removal, imported blankets cost N$200 and home blankets N$210, and the number of blanket brands in the shops rose from 6 to 14. Explain how consumers in this economy gain from the removal, using the figures.
items.canonical_answer: The imported blanket falls from N$250 to N$200 and the home blanket from N$240 to N$210, because home makers can no longer price under a tariff-sheltered import: consumers save N$250 - N$200 = N$50 on an import and N$240 - N$210 = N$30 on a home blanket. Brands rise from 6 to 14, so varieties the tariff kept out now reach the shops. Removing the tariff has therefore given consumers lower prices and wider choice.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - N$250 to N$200, N$240 to N$210, brands from 6 to 14 - and treat them as the evidence, not as decoration.
Reasoning: each gain needs its because link - prices fall because import competition returns, choice widens because varieties kept out by the tariff enter.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean for consumers: the same blanket costs less, and there are more blankets to choose between.

items.prompt: At the border post at Walvis Bay, officials add a charge of N$50 to each imported blanket that crosses. Define a tariff.
items.canonical_answer: A tariff is a government tax on imported goods. It raises the import's price in the home market - the N$50 charge lifts an N$200 blanket to N$250 - and the government collects it as revenue. Unlike a quota, it works through price, not quantity.
marking_guidance: Definition: the precise meaning required is a tax on imported goods; the example may earn the second mark alongside it.
The boundary worth a word: a tariff taxes each import and raises revenue, whereas a quota caps the quantity directly - naming the difference shows the term is understood rather than pattern-matched.

items.prompt: A government can shelter home blanket makers with a tariff or with an import quota. Explain why a quota may protect them more strongly than a tariff.
items.canonical_answer: A quota caps the quantity imported directly, whatever buyers are willing to pay. A tariff works through price: it lifts the import price, but if buyers keep buying - because they prefer the imported make or home supply is short - imports keep entering and the shelter leaks. Because a quota fixes the quantity, home producers keep the sales it reserves for them however strongly buyers want the import. So the quota removes the buyer's choice that a tariff leaves open.
marking_guidance: Reasons: the reason required is the mechanism - a quota fixes the quantity whatever the price, a tariff only raises it - developed with a because link.
Why: the development should show what happens where buyers keep paying - the tariff shelter weakens while the quota holds - since that is what stronger protection means.

items.prompt: Namibia places an N$80 tariff on each imported shirt, which costs N$320 at the border before the tariff. In the following year imports fall from 20 000 shirts to 15 000, and home shirt makers raise output from 9 000 shirts to 12 000. Explain how the tariff has protected home shirt makers, using the figures.
items.canonical_answer: The tariff raises the imported shirt from N$320 to N$400, since N$320 + N$80 = N$400, so home shirts become cheaper relative to the import. Buyers respond: imports fall from 20 000 to 15 000 shirts, and home output rises from 9 000 to 12 000, which is 12 000 - 9 000 = 3 000 more shirts. The tariff has protected home makers because the dearer import turns buyers towards home shirts, raising their output and sales.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - the N$80 tariff on the N$320 shirt, imports 20 000 to 15 000, home output 9 000 to 12 000 - as the working material.
Reasoning: the protection needs its because link - the tariff raises the import price, so buyers shift towards home shirts, so home output rises.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean for home shirt makers: 3 000 more shirts made and sold, because the import stands N$80 dearer.

items.prompt: Namibia's solar panel industry started only recently and cannot yet match the prices of panels from established producers abroad. Define an infant industry.
items.canonical_answer: An infant industry is a new domestic industry not yet large enough to produce at the cost per unit of established foreign rivals, so it cannot yet compete on price. Protection may shelter it until it grows to the scale at which its costs fall.
marking_guidance: Meaning: the definition must state a new domestic industry, too small to match established rivals on cost per unit, and may add the temporary shelter of protection while it grows.
The reason it names: infant industry is one of the reasons governments give for protection, so the definition should carry why it is newness that matters - scale has not yet brought costs down.

items.prompt: Imported solar panels cost N$340 each before Namibia places an N$80 tariff on them to shelter its three-year-old panel industry. Analyse how the tariff may help the infant industry reach the scale it needs, and who bears the cost while it grows.
items.canonical_answer: The tariff raises an imported panel from N$340 to N$420, since N$340 + N$80 = N$420. Home panels priced between those two figures now undercut the import, so buyers who mind price switch and home firms keep sales they would have lost. With sales held, output grows, and as output grows the cost per unit tends to fall because costs are spread over more panels - the scale the industry needs to face imports without shelter one day. Home panel firms and their workers gain sales and jobs; consumers bear the cost, paying up to N$80 more a panel until the industry matures and the tariff is withdrawn.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the analysis must open with the initial change - the tariff lifting the imported panel from N$340 to N$420 - before any consequence is drawn.
Mechanism: the middle marks are for the causal chain - the dearer import turns buyers towards home panels, so home sales and output grow, so cost per unit falls with scale.
Consequence: the chain must land somewhere: the industry moves towards competing without shelter, and the marks follow the therefore, not the listing.
For whom: the answer must name who gains - home firms and workers - and who bears the cost - consumers paying more per panel while the industry grows.

items.prompt: Cement arrives at Walvis Bay priced below the cost of producing it, and home cement makers see their sales fall from 60 000 tonnes a year to 40 000 within a year. Explain why these figures may lead the government to protect the cement industry.
items.canonical_answer: Cement priced below its cost of production suggests dumping: a seller taking the Namibian market at a loss home makers cannot match. Home sales fell by a third in a year, from 60 000 to 40 000 tonnes, and because the losses continue, home makers may close, leaving the country dependent on the sellers who drove them out. The government may therefore protect the industry with a tariff or quota, because raising the dumped price or capping its quantity keeps the home market, its jobs and secure supply.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - sales falling from 60 000 tonnes to 40 000 a year, and the below-cost price - as the evidence of dumping.
Reasoning: protection follows from the reason, not the figures alone: below-cost selling is dumping, so the government acts because uncounted losses lead home producers to close.
Conclusion: the answer should close with what the figures mean: a dumped import is taking the market, and protection is the reply that keeps the home industry standing.

items.prompt: After one country placed a tariff on Namibian beef, Namibia replied with a tariff on that country's machinery. Define a retaliatory tariff.
items.canonical_answer: A retaliatory tariff is a tariff one country places on another country's goods in answer to a barrier that country has placed on its exports. It is a consequence of the first barrier, and each round tends to shrink trade between the two.
marking_guidance: Definition: the precise meaning required is a tariff imposed in response to another country's trade barrier - both halves, the tariff and the reply, are needed.
The direction to keep: the retaliation is a consequence of the first barrier, and the answer should carry that direction rather than presenting the reply as a fresh grievance.

items.prompt: The N$80 tariff on imported shirts, which cost N$320 at the border before the tariff, has now run for two years. Imports stand at 15 000 shirts a year against 20 000 before the tariff, and home output at 12 000 against 9 000. Analyse the consequences of the tariff for consumers, home shirt makers and the government.
items.canonical_answer: The tariff keeps an imported shirt at N$400 against N$320 before, and the market has settled at 15 000 imported and 12 000 home-made shirts. Because the import is dearer, buyers pay N$80 more for an imported shirt, and home shirts, less undercut, tend to rise in price too. Consumers therefore pay more and choose from fewer imports. Home makers produce 12 000 - 9 000 = 3 000 more shirts a year and keep the jobs behind them, though the shelter weakens their pressure to cut costs. The government collects 15 000 x N$80 = N$1 200 000 a year, a transfer from buyers to the state rather than new wealth.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the analysis must open with the standing situation - the N$80 tariff, imports at 15 000, home output at 12 000 - before the consequences are drawn.
Mechanism: the chain must show because the import is dearer, prices and quantities settle where they do, and therefore each party lands where the figures show.
Consequence: each consequence must arrive as a result - consumers pay more, home makers hold 3 000 more shirts of output, the government collects N$1 200 000 a year.
For whom: the three parties must be named - consumers, home shirt makers, the government - and the marks follow the consequence for each rather than a list of prices.

items.prompt: Namibia's shirt industry employs 2 000 workers behind the N$80 tariff. Discuss whether the country should keep protecting it.
items.canonical_answer: Keeping it might be right: 2 000 workers and their households depend on the industry, and because the tariff holds the import N$80 dearer, home output and those jobs stay; sheltered, an industry not yet at scale may grow until it can compete without help. It might be wrong: consumers pay N$80 more for an imported shirt and home shirts tend to cost more too, so the cost spreads across every household that buys shirts; the shelter removes the pressure to cut costs, so an industry that never matures may lean on the tariff indefinitely; and the partner loses exports and may retaliate against Namibia's own sales, such as fish or beef, so both countries trade less. On balance the protection is worth keeping where the industry is genuinely moving towards standing alone. What settles it is whether the tariff is temporary, with a stated point of withdrawal: where none exists, the consumer cost and the retaliation risk decide the case against.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer must reach a reasoned conclusion - on balance, or it depends - not a list of points.
Why it might: the argument for keeping the protection must be developed - the 2 000 jobs, the time to reach scale.
Why it might not: the argument against must be developed with its own weight - the consumer cost, the missing pressure to improve, the retaliation on Namibia's exports.

Decisive: what settles it is the condition - whether the tariff is temporary and the industry genuinely maturing, and the strongest answers state what would have to hold for protection to be worth its cost.

items.prompt: A mining multinational with its head office abroad opens a copper mine near Tsumeb, employing 900 workers. Analyse the costs this multinational may bring to Namibia as the host country.
items.canonical_answer: Because the mine's owners are abroad, much of its profit is sent back to the home country, so income created in Namibia leaves the economy. Mining may damage land and water near Tsumeb and uses up a non-renewable resource, which leads to costs for local farmers and future generations. Local firms competing for workers or supplies may lose out to a far larger rival. If copper prices fall, the MNC may close the mine and concentrate on its mines in other countries, so the 900 workers and the town's suppliers lose their income. It may also press the government for tax breaks, cutting government revenue.
marking_guidance: Limitation: the costs to the host must be identified - profits sent abroad, environmental damage and resource depletion, local firms losing out, the risk of a sudden closure, or pressure for tax breaks.
Because: the link must be made from each cost to its effect - for example, profit sent abroad leads to income leaving the economy.
For whom: the consequence must land on named agents - the 900 workers, local farmers and firms, and the government.

items.prompt: Kalahari Retail, a supermarket chain with its head office in Windhoek, opens 20 stores in Zambia and Angola that earn profits of N$30 million a year. Analyse the benefits of these operations to Namibia as the home country.
items.canonical_answer: Because the profits of N$30 million a year are sent back to Windhoek, Namibia's national income rises, shareholders gain and the government may tax the profits. Selling in two more countries gives the firm a larger market, so it can buy in bulk at a lower cost per unit, which leads to growth that keeps skilled head-office jobs in buying, finance and management in Windhoek. Namibian suppliers may also sell to the foreign stores. So the government, shareholders, head-office workers and Namibian suppliers benefit.
marking_guidance: Benefit: the advantage to the home country must be identified - profits returned, a larger market, head-office jobs, or sales by home suppliers.
Because: the link must be made - profit sent home leads to higher national income and tax revenue; a larger market leads to bulk buying and growth.
For whom: the consequence must land on named agents - the government, shareholders, head-office workers and suppliers.

items.prompt: Explain why a multinational company that moves its factory from its home country to a host country may harm the home country.
items.canonical_answer: The factory's jobs move abroad, so workers in the home country may become unemployed, and the town that depended on the factory loses income and spending. The investment in new plant is also made abroad rather than at home. The home government loses the tax it collected on those wages and, where profits are booked in a lower-tax host, on profits too. Exports may fall, because the foreign plant now supplies markets that home factories once served.
marking_guidance: Reason: because production jobs and investment move abroad, home workers and the town around the factory lose income.
Reason: because wages, and possibly profits, are now earned abroad, the home government loses tax revenue and home exports may fall.

items.prompt: A beef producer near Gobabis gains tariff-free access to markets in Europe and China, and can now import its packaging machinery without tariffs. Analyse the benefits of free trade for this producer.
items.canonical_answer: Free trade gives the producer far more buyers than Namibia's 3 million people offer. Because it can sell more, it can produce on a larger scale, which leads to a lower cost per unit and higher profit. Importing machinery without tariffs lowers its costs further and gives access to better technology. Facing foreign rivals also pushes it to become more efficient so that it keeps its buyers. The firm, its owners and its workers benefit, and the cattle farmers who supply it gain a larger, steadier market.
marking_guidance: Benefit: the advantage to the producer must be identified - larger markets, cheaper inputs and technology, or pressure to become more efficient.
Because: the link must be made - more sales lead to larger-scale production and a lower cost per unit; tariff-free machinery lowers costs.
For whom: the consequence must land on named agents - the firm, its owners, its workers and the farmers who supply it.

items.prompt: A country removes its tariffs and import quotas on trade with its neighbours. Analyse how this free trade may benefit the economy as a whole.
items.canonical_answer: When barriers are removed, goods flow more freely both ways. Because each country can now sell more of what it produces at lowest cost, resources shift towards those industries, so total output tends to rise. This causes exports to grow, earning foreign currency and creating jobs, while competition from imports holds prices down and pushes home firms to be more efficient. Foreign firms may also invest, bringing technology. Therefore output, employment and efficiency tend to rise, though firms that cannot compete may close. Workers, firms, consumers and the government, through higher tax revenue, are affected.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - tariffs and quotas removed on trade with neighbours - must be stated.
Mechanism: because resources shift to the industries where the country produces at lowest cost, this causes output and exports to rise and competition to sharpen efficiency.
Consequence: therefore output, employment and efficiency in the economy tend to rise, with firms that cannot compete at risk.
For whom: workers, firms, consumers and the government must be named.

items.prompt: Country G, a high-income country, exports cars and machinery and imports clothing and raw materials. Country M, a low-income country, earns 60% of its export revenue from tobacco and tea and imports machinery and fuel. Using this information, explain why the benefits of free trade may differ between the two countries.
items.canonical_answer: G can sell manufactured exports and buy clothing and raw materials more cheaply. M gains buyers for its crops and access to machinery and fuel. However, with 60% of M's export receipts from tobacco and tea, its receipts are exposed to changes in those crop prices and harvests. Less diverse exports may make its gains less stable, while new industries may face strong import competition. The information does not establish which country gains more overall; that depends on prices, costs, demand and how gains are shared.
marking_guidance: Context: use G's manufactured exports and M's 60% export concentration in tobacco and tea.
Reasoning: because the export mixes differ, access to wider markets and exposure to crop prices and harvests can differ.
Conclusion: M may face less stable gains, but the supplied information cannot rank the total gains for the two countries.

items.prompt: Home boot makers in Mariental need to charge N$360 a pair to cover their costs, while imported boots sell at N$330 a pair. The government pays home makers a subsidy of N$45 for each pair they make. Using the figures, explain how the subsidy protects home boot makers.
items.canonical_answer: Before the subsidy, home boots at N$360 cost N$30 more than imports at N$330, so buyers tend to choose imports. The subsidy lowers home makers' costs by N$45 a pair, so they can charge N$360 - N$45 = N$315, now N$15 below the import price. Home makers can keep or win back buyers, protecting their output and jobs, while the import price is unchanged. The cost falls on taxpayers rather than buyers, since the government pays N$45 for every pair made at home.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures must anchor the answer - N$360 against N$330 before, the N$45 subsidy, and the new home price of N$315.
Reasoning: because the subsidy lowers home makers' costs without touching the import price, the link to home boots becoming cheaper than imports must be given.
Conclusion: therefore home makers keep their buyers, output and jobs, with the cost borne by taxpayers.

items.prompt: Define an embargo.
items.canonical_answer: An embargo is a ban on trade, either with a particular country or in a particular product, so that the goods concerned may not be imported or exported at any price.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must name a ban on trade with a country or in a product; a tax on imports defines a tariff and a limit on quantity defines a quota.

items.prompt: A clothing mill in Okahandja employs 1 200 of the town's workers, but its sales have fallen by 15% a year for three years as cheaper imported clothing arrives. Using this information, explain why the government might protect this declining industry.
items.canonical_answer: With sales falling 15% a year for three years, the mill is losing its market to imports and may close suddenly. Its 1 200 workers are a large share of Okahandja's jobs, so a sudden closure would raise unemployment and cut spending in the town's shops. A tariff or quota for a limited period would slow the decline, giving workers time to retrain and the town time to attract new employers. The cost is higher clothing prices for consumers, and the case weakens if the protection stays in place indefinitely.
marking_guidance: Context: the information must anchor the answer - sales falling 15% a year for three years and 1 200 workers in one town.
Reasoning: because a sudden closure would raise unemployment in a town that depends on the mill, the link from protection to a slower decline and time to retrain must be given.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must close on why protection may be justified for a limited period, with its cost to consumers.

items.prompt: Explain why a government may protect a strategic industry such as maize growing.
items.canonical_answer: Maize is a staple food, so a country that relied fully on imports could face shortages if supply were cut by war, drought in exporting countries or an export ban by a supplier. Protecting home growers with tariffs, quotas or subsidies keeps the land, skills and equipment to produce maize at home, so the population can still be fed in a crisis. The cost is that consumers or taxpayers tend to pay more in normal times than imports would cost.
marking_guidance: Reason: because imports of a staple food could be cut by war, drought abroad or an export ban, relying on them risks shortages.
Reason: because protection keeps the capacity to grow maize at home, supply is secured in a crisis, at a cost to consumers or taxpayers in normal times.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Globalisation is best defined as:
A  the spread of multinational companies across the world
B  the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, companies and the movement of finance, information and people
C  the removal of all border taxes everywhere
D  the movement of workers from poorer countries to richer ones

2. A multinational company is a firm that:
A  is owned by the government of its home country
B  sells its shares on a stock exchange
C  exports everything it produces
D  produces goods or services in more than one country

3. Free trade means:
A  goods cross borders and buyers pay nothing for them
B  trade between neighbouring countries only
C  international trade without government barriers such as tariffs and quotas
D  trade carried by sea rather than by road or air

4. Which is a benefit of free trade for consumers?
A  lower prices and wider choice as imports compete with home goods
B  more tariff revenue for the government
C  larger markets for home producers
D  higher prices that reward home firms for their quality

5. A tariff is:
A  a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
B  a tax on imported goods
C  a payment to home producers that lowers their costs
D  a ban on trade with a particular country

6. An import quota differs from a tariff because a quota:
A  raises revenue for the government on each unit
B  lowers the price of the imported good at the border
C  removes the barrier once home producers are ready
D  caps the quantity imported directly, whatever the price

7. A government shelters a new industry until it grows big enough to produce at a cost per unit close to established rivals. The reason for protection named here is:
A  declining industry
B  dumping
C  infant industry
D  strategic industry

8. A tariff of N$80 is placed on 15 000 imported shirts a year. The revenue it raises is:
A  N$120 000
B  N$12 000
C  N$2 400 000
D  N$1 200 000
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 D, 3 C, 4 A, 5 B, 6 D, 7 C, 8 D.
1. B states the definition - growing integration through trade, companies and movement. A narrows globalisation to one carrier of it, C mistakes a policy choice some countries make for the whole process, D names one flow among several and misses trade, companies and finance.
2. D is the definition - produces in more than one country, through operations it runs there. A confuses a multinational with a state-owned company, B with a public limited company - the confusion between where it operates and who owns it - and C describes an exporter: selling abroad from a home base does not make a firm multinational.
3. C states it - trade without government barriers. A is the free trade vs goods being free confusion: free refers to the barriers, not to the price. B mistakes the reach of trade for its freedom, and D mistakes the mode of transport for the policy.
4. A names the consumer benefit - lower prices and wider choice. B answers at the level of the government and C at the level of producers, which is the individuals vs country confusion: the question names consumers, and D reverses the direction of the benefit.
5. B is the definition - a tax on imports. A is the quota, C the subsidy, D the embargo: three of the four methods of protection, swapped for the one asked for.
6. D gives the difference - a quota caps quantity directly. A describes a tariff, not a quota; B reverses what a border barrier does; C invents a self-removing barrier, and the persistent answer is that a quota holds whatever the price.
7. C - new industry growing towards scale is the infant industry. A is an industry losing ground, B is an exporter pricing below cost, D is security of supply: each is a different reason, and the scale argument names the infant.
8. D - 15 000 x N$80 = N$1 200 000. A drops a zero in the multiplication, B drops two, and C doubles it: each is an arithmetic slip rather than a different method.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question; the correct option for each question is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Distractors that merely restate the question catch nothing; each wrong option traces to a named error - an ownership form read as multinationality, free trade read as goods without price, a consumer benefit answered at the producer or government level, or one protection method swapped for another.

items.prompt:
A report from Otavi, 2026. Namibia's blanket makers asked two years ago for shelter against imported blankets, and the government replied with a tariff of N$50 on each imported blanket. The figures below show the blanket market in the year before the tariff and last year. Home blanket makers have since raised output from 3 000 to 3 800 blankets.

Table 1 - blankets a year
  imported, year before the tariff: 8 000 blankets at N$200 each
  imported, last year: 6 000 blankets at N$250 each
  home-made, year before the tariff: 3 000 blankets at N$210 each
  home-made, last year: 3 800 blankets at N$230 each
  tariff: N$50 on each imported blanket

(a) Calculate the price of an imported blanket once the tariff is added to the N$200 border price. [1]
(b) Calculate the tariff revenue the government collected last year. [1]
(c) Identify two methods of protection, other than a tariff, the government could have used. [2]
(d) Explain why the tariff may help home blanket makers. [4]
(e) Analyse what the figures suggest the tariff has done to consumers, home producers and the government in Namibia, and how the exporting country's blanket makers may respond. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) N$200 + N$50 = N$250. The imported blanket costs the buyer N$250 once the tariff is added.
(b) 6 000 x N$50 = N$300 000. The government collected N$300 000 of tariff revenue last year.
(c) An import quota - a limit on the quantity of blankets that may be imported - and a subsidy - a payment to home blanket makers that lowers their costs. A subsidy lets home makers price closer to the import without the import price rising, with the cost falling on taxpayers. An embargo - a ban on blanket imports - would also earn credit as a third method; it stops the trade altogether.
(d) The tariff adds N$50 to each imported blanket, so the import rises from N$200 to N$250 while home blankets sell at N$230. Because the home blanket is now N$20 cheaper than the import, buyers who mind price tend to switch, so home makers keep and grow their sales - output has risen from 3 000 to 3 800 blankets - and the jobs and income behind those sales stay in Otavi. The tariff helps home blanket makers because it lifts the price of the rival they compete against, which means that their own price wins buyers it was losing before.
(e) A tariff raises the import price and shifts buying towards home producers, while collecting revenue for the government. In the data, imports fell from 8 000 blankets to 6 000 while the import price rose from N$200 to N$250; home output rose from 3 000 to 3 800 while the home price rose from N$210 to N$230; the government collected N$300 000. Consumers pay the rise twice over - N$50 more for an imported blanket, and N$20 more for a home one, because import competition no longer holds the home price down - so the cost lands on buyers across the market, while the benefit concentrates on home producers and the state. Home producers gain 800 blankets of output, since 3 800 - 3 000 = 800, and with it the jobs behind them. The exporting country's blanket makers have lost 2 000 blankets of sales, since 8 000 - 6 000 = 2 000, and their likely response is to press their own government for barriers on Namibian exports, which would shrink trade on both sides. However, the figures suggest rather than prove - the home output gain may owe something to a colder season or new home capacity, and the price rises to something other than the tariff - so the tariff's share of each change is an inference, not an observation.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) and (b) are 1 mark each and must be exact calculations from Table 1; (c) is 2 marks, one per method named; (d) is 4 marks; (e) is 6 marks.
In (e) award one point per distinct linked statement: expected relationship, evidence from the data, analysis, and an exception all carry marks.
In (e) quoting a figure from Table 1 is evidence, not analysis - a figure without the linked statement it supports earns nothing in (e).
For whom: consequences in (e) are named for consumers, home producers, the government and the exporting country makers.

items.prompt:
Namibia trades freely in most goods but protects its three-year-old solar panel industry.
(a) Define the economic term free trade. [2]
(b) Explain two reasons why a government protects an industry from import competition. [4]
(c) Analyse how a tariff on imported solar panels may affect consumers, home panel makers and the government. [6]
(d) Discuss whether protecting an industry from imports benefits a country more than trading freely. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Free trade is international trade without government barriers - no tariffs, no import quotas, no embargoes. The word free refers to the barriers, not to prices: goods traded freely still carry prices and their buyers still pay them.
(b) Reason one, infant industry: a new industry starts small, so its cost per unit tends to sit above established foreign rivals; protection lifts the import price, so home firms keep sales while they grow towards the scale at which their costs fall. Reason two, anti-dumping: where an exporter sells below its cost of production to take the market, home producers lose sales and may close; a tariff or quota raises the dumped price, so home producers keep their market and their workers keep their jobs.
(c) The tariff raises the price of imported panels at the border. Because the import is dearer, buyers tend to switch towards home panels, so home makers keep sales they were losing and may raise output, while the jobs behind the output stay. Consumers pay more for a panel, imported or home, because import competition no longer holds the home price down; home panel makers gain output, sales and room to grow, though the shelter also eases the pressure on them to cut costs; the government collects the tariff as revenue, a transfer from buyers to the state. In short, consumers carry the cost, home makers and their workers hold the benefit, the government holds the revenue.
(d) Why it might benefit more: protection keeps home output and jobs that freer trade may move abroad, which matters where the industry employs whole towns; it gives an infant industry time to reach scale, after which the country may produce competitively without shelter; and it keeps supply secure where the good is strategic, such as food or fuel. Why it might not: consumers across the economy pay higher prices so that one industry can keep its sales, and the cost lands on every household that buys the good; the shelter removes the pressure on home firms to cut costs and improve, so an industry that never matures leans on the tariff indefinitely; and trading partners lose exports and may retaliate with barriers of their own, so the country ends up trading less on both sides; and protection gives up what free trade offers producers - cheaper inputs from abroad and larger markets - and the economy, whose resources shift towards what it produces best. Judgement: on balance protection benefits a country more than free trade where the shelter is genuinely temporary and the industry is moving towards standing alone - the condition it depends on - while where the protection settles into permanence, the consumer cost, the lost pressure to improve and the retaliation risk leave free trade the better servant of the country as a whole.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) 2 marks for two creditable elements of the definition; (b) 4 marks, two per reason developed with its because link; (c) 6 marks, one per distinct linked statement with its reason carried; (d) 8 marks, level-marked over three bands.

Bands for (d): Level 3 (top) examines why it might and why it might not, then reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side of the case; Level 1 asserts points without development.
In (c) the parties must be named - consumers, home panel makers, the government - and each consequence must arrive as a result rather than a list.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "A country that protects its industries from imports serves its people better than one that trades freely." Discuss. Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for protection:
Point 1 - jobs kept. Chain: a tariff lifts the import price -> buyers shift towards home goods -> home output and the jobs behind it stay -> the towns those industries employ keep their income (for workers and their households).
Point 2 - time to reach scale. Chain: an infant industry starts small, so its cost per unit sits above rivals -> shelter holds the import price up -> home firms keep sales while they grow -> costs per unit tend to fall with scale -> the industry may one day stand without shelter (for the industry and the economy).
Case against protection:
Point 1 - consumers pay. Chain: the import price rises -> home prices follow as import competition eases -> households pay more for the same goods -> the cost spreads across every buyer of the good (for consumers, and low-income households hardest).
Point 2 - the reply from abroad. Chain: partner exporters lose sales -> their government may retaliate with barriers of its own -> the country's exporters lose the markets they had -> trade shrinks on both sides (for exporters and the economy).
Judgement: protection serves the people better where the shelter is genuinely temporary - where the industry is moving to stand alone and the tariff has a stated end - and the condition it depends on is whether that withdrawal is realistic. Where the protection settles into permanence, the permanent consumer cost and the retaliation risk mean the people are served better by trading freely, with protection kept for the narrow cases of dumping and strategic supply.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the case for, the case against and the stated judgement is what is assessed.
Each point must be developed as a chain from the barrier to its consequence, naming the party it lands on - workers, consumers, exporters, the economy.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: whether the protection is temporary and the industry genuinely maturing.
What settles it: what the shelter buys and whether it is withdrawn once it has bought it - the decisive test is the realistic exit, not the shelter itself.

facts: protection via tariff lifts import price
free trade lowers consumer prices through import competition
